findings.description: A password is hashed for storage, or a key derived from it, with PBKDF2, and the number of rounds written into the code is below what OWASP recommends: 600,000 for SHA-256 and 210,000 for SHA-512 (SHA-1 needs 1,300,000). A count below 210,000 is reported whatever the hash; one below 600,000 where the call itself names SHA-256, and one below 1,300,000 where it names SHA-1.
findings.fix: Raise the number of rounds to at least 600,000 for PBKDF2 with SHA-256 (210,000 with SHA-512, and 1,300,000 with SHA-1, which is better replaced), or use a password hashing function made for this, such as Argon2id or scrypt. Keep the count where it can be raised later without breaking what was already stored.
findings.impact: Anyone who gets hold of what the key protects, such as an encrypted backup, an export, or a stored hash, can try guesses at the password quickly on ordinary hardware, and most people's passwords fall to a fast guesser.
findings.title: A password is stored, or a key made from it, with too few rounds of work

questions_for_you.how: For each kind of information people type into the app (names, email addresses, dates, amounts, free text), write down the validation rules: what a valid value looks like, how long it may be, and what the app does with one that is not valid.
questions_for_you.plain: For each thing people type into the app (a name, an email address, a date, an amount), what does a good one look like, how long may it be, and what should the app do with one that is wrong?
questions_for_you.title: What counts as valid input
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Go through every form and every field an API accepts, and for each one write what a good value looks like. The quickest way to find them all is to open each page that has a form and list its inputs.

questions_for_you.how: How the app defends against someone trying many passwords (password brute force) or leaked email and password pairs (credential stuffing): rate limiting, delays, or lockout, and the numbers, such as five failed attempts in fifteen minutes. Say how these controls are configured, and how the app stops an attacker locking a real person out on purpose (malicious account lockout).
questions_for_you.plain: After how many wrong passwords in a row does the app slow down or lock the account, and for how long? And how does it stop somebody locking a real person out on purpose? (Say the numbers you want, even if the app does not do it yet.)
questions_for_you.title: How sign-in is protected against guessing
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Look in your sign-in code for anything that counts failures — a rate limiter, a lockout, a delay. If you find nothing, that is the answer, and the number to write down is the one you want rather than the one you have.

questions_for_you.how: The authorization rules: which kinds of users may use which functions (function-level: only administrators may open the admin page), and which records each may see or change (data-specific: a person may only open their own notes).
questions_for_you.plain: Who may do what in the app: which kinds of people may use which features, and whose records may each one see or change?
questions_for_you.title: Who may do what
questions_for_you.where_to_look: List the kinds of user the app has, then walk through the app as each one and note what they can reach. The pages that only some people should see, and the records that belong to one person, are what these rules are about.

questions_for_you.how: Time frames for remediation: how soon a third-party library with a known vulnerability is updated, by how serious the vulnerability is (for example, critical within a week), and how often libraries are updated in general.
questions_for_you.plain: When a library the app uses turns out to have a security hole, how soon must it be updated, by how serious the hole is (critical within a week, say)? And how often are libraries updated anyway?
questions_for_you.title: How quickly outdated libraries are updated
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Decide the number of days you would accept between a vulnerability being published and it being fixed, for each level of severity. Start from how bad it would be for this app rather than from what other people write down. Then put the same numbers in stackvet.toml as `[policy] fix-within-days`, so `sv audit` can hold the app's packages to them.

questions_for_you.how: Does the application enforce input validation on the server — a trusted service layer — and not only in the browser? Client-side validation improves usability and should be kept, but anyone can skip it by sending a request straight to the server, so it settles nothing on its own.
questions_for_you.plain: When someone types something into a form, does the server check it before using it, and not only the page in their browser (which anyone can skip)?
questions_for_you.title: Input validation is enforced at a trusted service layer
questions_for_you.where_means: the file where input validation happens on the server
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Find where the app receives a form or an API request, and look at what happens to the values before they are used. If the only checks you find are in the browser — HTML attributes, JavaScript — that is the answer.

questions_for_you.how: Does the application perform all session token verification using a trusted backend service, rather than believing something the browser sends about who is signed in?
questions_for_you.plain: When the app decides who is signed in, does the server check that against something it issued itself, rather than taking the browser's word for it?
questions_for_you.title: Session tokens are verified by a trusted backend service
questions_for_you.where_means: the file where the session is verified
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Find the code that runs on every request and decides who is signed in. Check whether it verifies something the server issued, or simply believes a value from a cookie or header.

questions_for_you.how: Does the application enforce its authorization rules at a trusted service layer — the server — rather than relying on controls an untrusted consumer could manipulate, such as a hidden button or a disabled field in the browser? Hiding a link is not a rule: anyone can request the address directly.
questions_for_you.plain: When somebody tries to open a page or do something they are not allowed to, is it the server that stops them, or only a button that is hidden?
questions_for_you.title: Authorization rules are enforced at a trusted service layer
questions_for_you.where_means: the file where authorization is enforced
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Take a page or an action only some people should reach, and find the code that stops everybody else. If the only thing you find is the button being hidden in the template, that is the answer.

questions_for_you.how: When the application returns a record, does it return only the required fields, rather than the whole object with fields the person should not see?
questions_for_you.plain: When the app sends a record to a page or another program, does it send only the parts that will be shown, and not the whole record with things that person should not see?
questions_for_you.title: Only the fields that are needed are sent back
questions_for_you.where_means: the file that decides which fields are returned
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Look at what an API returns for one record, or what a page sends to the browser, and compare it with what is shown. Anything extra in the response is being sent and simply not displayed.

questions_for_you.how: Take a flow with more than one step — checkout, sign-up with a confirmation, anything with a "next" button. Write down the address of the last step. Start the flow again, and go straight to that address without doing the steps before it. It should refuse. Then try the steps in the wrong order, and try the same step twice. Describing the flow in stackvet.toml as `flow` under `[stack.run.users]` lets `sv report --run` try two skips, one wrong order, and one repeated step for you; other orders, and the last step sent again after the flow finished, are still yours.
questions_for_you.title: Steps cannot be skipped or done out of order

questions_for_you.how: Open the live site in a browser and click the padlock. It should show a certificate issued by a public authority, with a date that has not passed, and the name should match the address. A warning page, or a certificate the app generated for itself, means no visitor can tell your site from an impostor.
questions_for_you.title: The certificate on the live site is one browsers trust

questions_for_you.how: Write the time frames from your security notes into stackvet.toml as `[policy] fix-within-days`, one number of days per severity, then run `sv report --advisories DIR` (or `sv audit`) against a local advisory database. It lists the packages with a known vulnerability and puts the ones past your time frame first. Those are the answer to this one. Without the numbers it counts every known vulnerability as late, whatever its age.
questions_for_you.title: Nothing is past the update deadline you set

questions_for_you.how: Look at how changes to the app get in: check that every change your AI coding tool wrote is read and approved by a qualified person before it goes live, and that the reviewer is not the same person who asked the AI for the code. The AI agent does not count as the human reviewer. If changes go straight from the AI to the live app, the answer is no.
questions_for_you.title: A person reviews the code the AI wrote

questions_for_you.how: List the places the app takes something typed or sent in that decides what happens next: an amount, a quantity, a date, a status, a role, a choice from a list. For each, try a value it should refuse: a negative or huge number, a date in the past, a word that is not one of the choices, an empty field. The app should refuse it with a message, not accept it and carry on. A form that only checks in the browser does not count: send the same value again with the browser's tools, or ask your AI coding tool to show you the check on the server.
questions_for_you.title: Input is checked against what the app expects

questions_for_you.how: Where two or more data items have to agree with each other once combined (a start date before an end date, a city that matches the ZIP code), write down which combinations matter and how the app checks that logical consistency.
questions_for_you.plain: Which things people enter have to make sense together (a start date before an end date, say), and how does the app check them?
questions_for_you.title: Data items that must make sense combined
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Open each form that takes more than one value and list the pairs that have to agree — two dates, a country and a postal code, a quantity and a maximum. For each, try the combination that should be impossible and see whether the app takes it.

questions_for_you.how: Write down the business logic limits: how many of something one person may create or do, and in how long (per user), and any limits across the whole app (globally), such as a daily total.
questions_for_you.plain: How many of something may one person make or do, and in how long? And is there any limit for the whole app, such as a total per day?
questions_for_you.title: Business limits
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Go through the app as a user and note everything somebody could do repeatedly: create a record, send an invitation, start an export. For each, decide the number that would be too many in a day, and write that down.

questions_for_you.how: For each place people can upload a file: the permitted file types and extensions, the maximum size (including once unpacked, for a zip), and how the app makes a file safe to download again, including what happens when a file looks malicious.
questions_for_you.plain: Where people can upload a file: which kinds of file are allowed, how big may one be (unpacked, for a zip), and what does the app do with a file that looks dangerous?
questions_for_you.title: What files people may upload
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Open each place the app takes a file and look at what the code accepts today: the extensions it allows, the size limit if there is one, and where the file ends up. Write down what it should be, which may not be what it is.

questions_for_you.how: A list of context-specific words people may not use in their passwords: the app's name, the organization's name, product names, and other words someone would guess first.
questions_for_you.plain: Which words should nobody be allowed to use in a password here, because they are the first anyone would guess (the app's name, your organization's name, your products)?
questions_for_you.title: Words not allowed in passwords
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Start from the names somebody could guess without knowing you: the app, your organization, your product, the town you are in. Add the obvious variations with numbers on the end.

questions_for_you.how: If there is more than one way to sign in (a password, a Google or Microsoft account, a code by email, an API key), list all these authentication pathways, and say which security controls apply to each, so they are enforced consistently and one is not weaker than the others.
questions_for_you.plain: What are all the ways someone can sign in (a password, a Google or Microsoft account, a code by email, a key for programs), and are they all protected as well as each other?
questions_for_you.title: Every way to sign in
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Open the sign-in page and list every button on it, then search the code for anywhere else a session is created — an API key check, a magic link, a mobile app, an admin back door. Each one is a pathway, and they should all be as strong as each other.

questions_for_you.how: The session inactivity timeout (how long someone can be away before signing in again) and the absolute maximum session lifetime (how long any session lasts at most), and why those times are right for this app. If they are longer than NIST SP 800-63B suggests, say why.
questions_for_you.plain: How long may someone be away before they have to sign in again, how long may anyone stay signed in at most, and why are those times right for this app?
questions_for_you.title: How long someone stays signed in
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Find the two numbers in your app's configuration: how long an idle session lasts, and how long any session lasts at most. If you cannot find them, the answer is whatever your framework does by default, and that is the number to write down and then reconsider.

questions_for_you.how: How many concurrent sessions one account may have at once (a phone and a laptop, say), and what the app does when someone reaches the maximum: sign out the oldest, refuse the new one, or tell the person.
questions_for_you.plain: How many devices may one person be signed in on at once, and what happens when they sign in on one more?
questions_for_you.title: Signed in on several devices at once
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Sign in to the same account from two browsers and see whether both keep working. That tells you what the app does today; write down what it should do.

questions_for_you.how: Where some fields of a record are more restricted than the record itself, the field-level access rules: who may read and who may write each field, and whether that depends on the record's state or status (a published order's total can no longer be changed).
questions_for_you.plain: Where some parts of a record are more private than the rest: who may see each part, who may change it, and does that change once the record is, say, published?
questions_for_you.title: Who may see or change each field
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Take a record with a field not everybody should see — a price, a note, an internal status. Write down who may read it and who may change it, and whether that depends on the record's state.

questions_for_you.how: The policy for cryptographic keys: where each key is kept, who can reach it, how often it is replaced, and what happens when one may have leaked, following a key management standard such as NIST SP 800-57 through each key's lifecycle.
questions_for_you.plain: For each secret key the app uses: where is it kept, who can get to it, how often is it replaced, and what happens if it may have leaked?
questions_for_you.title: How keys are looked after
questions_for_you.where_to_look: List every key the app uses: session signing, encryption at rest, the TLS certificate, anything a provider gave you. For each, write where it lives, who can read it, and what you would do tomorrow if it leaked.

questions_for_you.how: A cryptographic inventory: every key, algorithm, and certificate the app uses, where each key may and may not be used, and what data each may and may not protect. Keep it updated when one is added or replaced.
questions_for_you.plain: What is every key, kind of encryption, and certificate the app uses, and what may each one be used for?
questions_for_you.title: Every key, algorithm, and certificate
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Look in your .env and your host's secret store, at the certificate on the live site, and at whatever the code calls to hash or encrypt. That is the inventory; write down which data each protects and where it may not be used.

questions_for_you.how: All the communication needs of the app: every external service it connects to (payment providers, email, AI services, other APIs) and why, and any place where someone using the app can give it an address that the app will then connect to itself.
questions_for_you.plain: What does the app connect to outside itself (payments, email, AI services, other programs), and why? And can anyone using the app give it an address that it will then visit itself?
questions_for_you.title: Everything the app talks to
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Look at your dependency list for anything that calls out — payment, email, AI, maps, analytics — and at the report's own list of outside services. Then add the places where somebody using the app can give it an address it will fetch.

questions_for_you.how: For each kind of sensitive data the app holds, its protection requirements: whether it is encrypted, how long it is kept (retention), whether and how it may appear in logs, who can see it, and anything the privacy law you follow requires.
questions_for_you.plain: For each kind of private information the app keeps: is it encrypted, how long is it kept, may it appear in logs, who can see it, and what does the privacy law you follow require?
questions_for_you.title: How each kind of sensitive data is protected
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Take each kind of data from the list you made for V14.1.1 and decide four things for it: encrypted or not, kept for how long, allowed in logs or not, and who may see it.

questions_for_you.how: Which functionality is time-consuming or resource-demanding (large exports, report generation, AI requests, image processing), and how the app prevents a loss of availability from overusing it: queues, limits per user, timeouts.
questions_for_you.plain: Which features are slow or heavy (big exports, reports, AI requests, image processing), and what stops one person's heavy use from making the app unavailable to everyone else?
questions_for_you.title: Slow or heavy features
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Time the slow things: an export, a report, a search over everything, an AI request, anything that resizes an image. Anything a person notices waiting for is what this asks about.

questions_for_you.how: An inventory of the logging: which events are logged, in what format, where the logs are stored, who can read them (access), what they are used for, and how long they are kept.
questions_for_you.plain: What does the app write in its logs, where are they kept, who can read them, what are they for, and how long are they kept?
questions_for_you.title: What the app logs
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Find where the app's output actually goes — the console, a file, your host's logging, an outside service — and what it writes at each level. Then say who can read it and how long it is kept.

questions_for_you.how: Is input decoded or unescaped into its final form exactly once, and before it is validated, rather than after? Decoding after the check lets something dangerous slip past a check that saw it encoded.
questions_for_you.plain: Where the app turns encoded text back into plain text (web addresses, base64, HTML), does it do that once, before checking the text, and never after?
questions_for_you.title: Input is decoded once, before it is checked
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Find where the app decodes what it receives — URL decoding, base64, unescaping HTML — and check whether that happens before or after the values are checked. Twice is also worth looking for.

questions_for_you.how: If a load balancer, proxy, or gateway sits in front of the application and adds header fields it relies on, can the application tell those apart from the same fields sent by a browser?
questions_for_you.plain: If something in front of the app (a load balancer, proxy, or gateway) adds information to each request that the app relies on, can the app tell that apart from the same information sent by a visitor?
questions_for_you.title: Headers added by a load balancer cannot be faked
questions_for_you.where_means: the file or configuration that handles those header fields
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Find out what sits in front of the app and which header fields it adds. Then search the code for those names, and check whether the app can tell one the proxy set from one a browser sent.

questions_for_you.how: Do all the components a request passes through — load balancers, firewalls, and the application server — agree on where one HTTP message ends and the next begins? When they disagree, somebody can hide a second request inside the first.
questions_for_you.plain: If a request passes through other machines before reaching the app (a load balancer, a firewall), do they all agree on where one request ends and the next begins?
questions_for_you.title: Everything in front of the app agrees where a request ends
questions_for_you.where_means: the configuration for the server or proxy in front of the app
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Find what sits in front of the app — a load balancer, a reverse proxy, your host's edge. Check whether each one and the app agree on request size limits, chunked encoding, and duplicate headers. If you run nothing in front of the app, say so: that is the answer.

questions_for_you.how: Where some fields of a record are more restricted than the record itself, does the application check permissions for those specific fields, both when read and when written?
questions_for_you.plain: Where some parts of a record are more private than the rest, does the app check who may see and who may change each of those parts, every time?
questions_for_you.title: Access to individual fields is restricted
questions_for_you.where_means: the file that enforces field-level permissions
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Take a record with a field not everybody should change, and find the code that saves it. Check whether it filters the fields it accepts, or takes whatever the request sends.

questions_for_you.how: Is the application designed so the algorithms, key lengths, and random number sources it uses for encryption and hashing can be replaced without rewriting it? Every algorithm in use now will eventually need replacing.
questions_for_you.plain: If one of the ways the app encrypts or scrambles data had to be swapped for a newer one, could that be done without rewriting the app?
questions_for_you.title: Encryption choices can be changed later
questions_for_you.where_means: the file where the algorithms are chosen
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Find where the app names an algorithm or a key length — hashing passwords, encrypting a field, signing a token. Check whether changing one would mean editing one place or many.

questions_for_you.how: Does the application prevent sensitive data from being kept in caches it does not own — a load balancer, a content delivery network, or an application cache — or make sure anything kept there is protected?
questions_for_you.plain: Is private information kept out of the caches the app does not control (your host's edge, a content delivery network), or protected when it is stored there?
questions_for_you.title: Sensitive data is not left in a cache
questions_for_you.where_means: the file or configuration that sets caching
questions_for_you.where_to_look: List every cache a response passes through: your host's edge or CDN, a reverse proxy, the browser. Then look at what a private page sends back in Cache-Control. Anything sensitive without no-store is the answer to this one.

questions_for_you.how: If proxies or middleware sit in front of the application, do they pass the visitor's original IP address in a field the visitor cannot set themselves? Rate limits and logs are worth nothing if the address can be chosen by whoever is being limited.
questions_for_you.plain: If anything sits between visitors and the app, does it pass on each visitor's real internet address in a way the visitor cannot fake?
questions_for_you.title: The visitor's real address is passed along truthfully
questions_for_you.where_means: the proxy configuration, or the file that reads the address
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Find out whether anything sits between the visitor and the app. If so, check which header field carries the real address and whether the app would believe the same field sent by a visitor directly.

questions_for_you.how: Do all the parts of the application that write logs keep their clocks synchronized, and do the timestamps use UTC or say which time zone they are in? Two logs with drifting clocks cannot be put in order after an incident.
questions_for_you.plain: Do all the parts of the app that keep logs have clocks that agree, and does every time they write say which time zone it is in?
questions_for_you.title: Clocks agree, and times say which zone they are in
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Look at a few recent log lines from each part of the app and compare their timestamps. Check whether they say which time zone they are in, and whether two parts logging the same moment agree.

questions_for_you.how: Are logs sent to a separate system, so that somebody who takes over the application cannot quietly delete the record of what they did?
questions_for_you.plain: Are the app's logs sent to a separate place, so someone who took over the app could not quietly delete them?
questions_for_you.title: Logs are sent somewhere separate
questions_for_you.where_means: the configuration that ships the logs
questions_for_you.where_to_look: Find where the logs end up. If the answer is a file on the same machine the app runs on, then somebody who takes over the app can edit them, and this is not done.

questions_for_you.how: `sv` does not check this: it takes dozens of connections to the live site, and `sv probe` keeps to four (the owner's decision, 6 October 2026). Run a scanner made for it against your live address, such as testssl.sh (`testssl.sh https://your-address`) or SSL Labs' free online test. The cipher list should show only ones rated strong or good, with forward secrecy, and no rating of weak, insecure, or vulnerable.
questions_for_you.title: The live site offers only strong encryption settings

questions_for_you.how: Take each limit from your security notes — so many of something per person, so many per day — and try to go past it in the app. Try it slowly and then quickly, and from two accounts at once if the limit is meant to be global.
questions_for_you.title: The business limits you wrote down are the ones the app enforces

questions_for_you.how: Only where something is limited in number: a seat, a slot, the last item in stock. Open the app in two browsers, get both to the moment of booking the same one, and confirm both as close together as you can. Exactly one should succeed.
questions_for_you.title: Two people cannot book the same thing

questions_for_you.how: Take a word from the list you wrote down — the app's name, your organization's name — and try to register an account using it as the password, or with it inside a longer password. It should be refused. Listing the words in stackvet.toml under `[policy]` as `context-words` lets `sv report --run` try the first one for you, through the app's own sign-up.
questions_for_you.title: The banned word list is actually used

questions_for_you.how: Try to register with a password known to have been breached. `Password123!` and `qwerty123456` will do; haveibeenpwned.com/Passwords lists more. The app should refuse it and say why, without telling the person anything about other accounts. `sv report --run` tries one such password through the app's own sign-up, but one refusal only supports this: it does not show the whole list is checked.
questions_for_you.title: Passwords from known breaches are refused

questions_for_you.how: Sign in and note everything you were asked for. A password alone is a single factor. A code from an app or a security key is a second one. If there is only a password, that is the answer to this one; if you have decided a password alone is enough, ASVS asks for the reasoning to be written down.
questions_for_you.title: Getting in needs more than a password

questions_for_you.how: List every way somebody can become signed in: the password form, any "sign in with" button, magic links by email, API keys, an admin back door, an old mobile app. Compare that with the list in your security notes. Anything not on the list is what this asks about, and each way in should be as strong as the others.
questions_for_you.title: There is no forgotten way in

questions_for_you.how: Only where people sign in with a second factor. Go through losing it as a person would: what does support ask for before restoring access? If the answer is less than what was asked when the account was set up, the recovery path is now the weakest way in.
questions_for_you.title: Losing a second factor does not become the easy way in

questions_for_you.how: Sign in, then leave the app alone for longer than the idle timeout you wrote down, without clicking anything. Come back and reload a private page. You should be asked to sign in again.
questions_for_you.title: Being away signs you out

questions_for_you.how: Sign in and keep using the app past the maximum lifetime you wrote down. Staying active must not keep it alive forever — at the limit you should be asked to sign in again even mid-use.
questions_for_you.title: A session does not last forever

questions_for_you.how: List where each password, key, and token the app needs actually comes from: a key vault or your host's secret store, an environment variable, or a file in the code. Say who can read each one, and how you would replace one if it leaked. A secret nobody can rotate is the answer to this one.
questions_for_you.title: Secrets live in something built to hold them

questions_for_you.how: From a browser that is not signed in, and ideally not on your network, try the addresses that exist for you rather than for visitors: /docs, /swagger, /metrics, /health, /debug, /admin, /.git. Each should either refuse or not exist.
questions_for_you.title: Nothing internal is reachable from outside

questions_for_you.how: List every kind of information the app stores, including what it writes to logs and what it keeps in backups. Mark each with how much it would matter if it got out. Anything you cannot place is the thing to look at, and remember that encoded is not the same as protected.
questions_for_you.title: You know which of your data is sensitive

questions_for_you.how: Open the app in a browser with the network panel recording, sign in, and use it normally. Look at every request going somewhere that is not your own address — analytics, error reporting, fonts, chat widgets. Check what is in each, including the address of the page, which often carries names or record numbers. With `browser` under `[stack.run.users]`, `sv report --run` looks through what the signed-in pages send to other sites for the test account's email address, password, and session cookie; but code a page loads from another site cannot run inside the fence, so what analytics and chat widgets send is still yours to look at.
questions_for_you.title: Nothing sensitive is handed to an outside service

questions_for_you.how: Take each protection you wrote down — encrypted, kept for so long, never in logs — and check the app against it. Search the logs for the data that should never appear there, and confirm that something really deletes records when their time is up.
questions_for_you.title: Sensitive data is handled the way your notes say

questions_for_you.how: Take each time-consuming or resource-demanding feature you documented — an export, a report, an AI request, image processing. Start several at once from one account and see whether the rest of the application stays usable. The defenses you wrote down should stop any one person causing a loss of availability for everybody else.
questions_for_you.title: Time-consuming features cannot cause a loss of availability

questions_for_you.how: Compare the log destinations in your inventory with where they really go: files on the server, your host's logging, any outside service, and anything printed to the console. A destination nobody wrote down is one nobody is watching or protecting.
questions_for_you.title: Logs go only where your inventory says

questions_for_you.how: Do each thing your notes say gets logged — a failed sign-in, a permission refused, a record deleted — then look in the logs and confirm each one is there with enough detail to tell who and when. Then try something that should be refused, such as posting a form with a field the app does not expect, and check that the refusal was logged too.
questions_for_you.title: The events you said would be logged really are

questions_for_you.how: Find where a file someone uploads is stored before anyone downloads it, and check whether it is scanned by antivirus software on the way in: your host's upload service may offer this, or a scanner such as ClamAV can be added. Try uploading the harmless EICAR test file, which every antivirus scanner recognizes. If the app accepts it and serves it back, known malicious content would be served too.
questions_for_you.title: Uploaded files are scanned for viruses

questions_for_you.how: Ask your AI coding tool to show you where the app decides how confident it is in an answer the model generated, before showing it. Look for a score or a check, not just the model's text passed straight through. If the answer is shown whatever the model said, the reliability of generated answers is not being assessed.
questions_for_you.title: The app judges how reliable each AI answer is

questions_for_you.how: With the confidence check from the item above, find the threshold below which an answer is not shown, and what the app shows instead: a fallback message such as "I'm not sure, please contact us". Try asking the AI something it cannot know about your business. It should fall back rather than invent an answer.
questions_for_you.title: A doubtful AI answer is blocked or replaced

questions_for_you.how: Check whether the app watches for conversations that look like probing: the same question retried many times with small changes, excessive retry attempts, or one visitor trying many different tricks in a row. Try it yourself and look for whether anything was flagged or anyone told.
questions_for_you.title: Unusual behavior toward the AI is spotted

questions_for_you.how: List the rules the app uses to recognize attacks aimed at the AI: jailbreak phrasings, prompt injection hidden in documents it reads, attempts to extract its system prompt. Try a few coordinated attempts from two accounts at once, and check whether the rules catch them and something is recorded.
questions_for_you.title: Jailbreak and prompt-injection attempts are recognized

questions_for_you.how: Check whether anyone regularly tries to trick the AI tools that help build the app: a pull request, issue, or comment with a hidden instruction, a known jailbreak, or a request to add a harmful package. Write down when this was last done and what it found, and whether each finding was tracked until fixed. If it has never been done, schedule the first red-team exercise.
questions_for_you.title: The AI coding tools themselves are attacked on purpose, on a schedule

questions_for_you.how: Ask your AI coding tool to list every place the app passes something a person typed into another program: a shell command, a file path, an email header, a spreadsheet export, a search sent elsewhere. For each, look at what it does to the input first. It should allow only the characters that place can safely take, and cut off input that is too long. Then try one: put a semicolon, a quote mark, or a very long line into that field, and check the result is refused or harmless.
questions_for_you.title: Input is cleaned before it reaches a dangerous place

questions_for_you.how: If the app gives people backup or recovery codes to sign in with, ask your AI coding tool to show you how they are stored. Open the database (or have the tool show you a row) and look at a stored code. It should be a long scrambled value made by a password hashing function such as bcrypt or Argon2, never the code itself. Try signing in with a code the app gave you: it should still work, which shows the scrambled value is checked rather than compared as written.
questions_for_you.title: Backup sign-in codes are stored scrambled, not as written

questions_for_you.how: Ask your AI coding tool to show you the line that makes each sign-in code, reset code, backup code, and two-factor secret. It should use the language's secure random source (`secrets` in Python, `crypto.randomInt` or `crypto.randomBytes` in JavaScript, `SecureRandom` in Java, `crypto/rand` in Go). `random`, `Math.random`, or a code made from the time or the user's id is the wrong answer. `sv check` finds the commonest wrong ones itself; this is for any it did not.
questions_for_you.title: Sign-in codes come from an unpredictable random source

questions_for_you.how: Ask your AI coding tool to list every place the app makes a key, a signing key, or a signature, and which method each uses. Look for RSA keys of at least 2048 bits (3072 is better), elliptic-curve keys on P-256 or Ed25519, and signatures made with SHA-256 or stronger. MD5, SHA-1, DSA, RSA under 2048 bits, or a key the app writes by hand from random bytes are the wrong answer. If the app makes no keys and signs nothing itself, write that down.
questions_for_you.title: Keys and signatures are made with approved methods

questions_for_you.how: List where the app's keys and passwords live (a hosting dashboard, a secrets manager, `.env` files, CI settings) and which parts of the app read each one. Check that each service, job, and person has access only to the ones it uses: the website should not hold the payment admin key, a test job should not see production keys, and a database login should not be an administrator unless it must be. `sv check` finds a CI workflow that hands every secret to a job; this covers the rest.
questions_for_you.title: Each part of the app can reach only the secrets it needs

questions_for_you.how: Open the app's logs where they are kept (the hosting dashboard, a log service, or the terminal it runs in). Then cause a few failures: stop the database briefly or give it a wrong password, send a request the app should refuse, and visit an address that makes it fail. Each should leave a line in the log saying what went wrong and when, without a password or key in it. Failures that leave no trace are the wrong answer.
questions_for_you.title: Unexpected errors and failed security checks are logged

requirement_text.AC.1.1: Verify that a written workflow says when AI tools may generate, refactor, or review code. The workflow names the approved tools, the prohibited use cases, and the data classifications that are allowed as input.
requirement_text.AC.1.2: Verify that the workflow covers every SSDLC phase from design and implementation through code review, testing, deployment, and post-deployment monitoring, and names the security gates that stay mandatory whether AI was involved or not.
requirement_text.AC.1.3: Verify that the workflow names the adversarial-AI threat scenarios it is built to mitigate. The list should cover prompt injection delivered through PR content, AI-generated supply-chain payloads, autonomous agents approving their own work, fork-PR secret exfiltration, and compromise of the model supply chain.
requirement_text.AC.10.1: Verify that AI-generated artifacts carry the required origin and generation fields: model identity and version, tool or agent identity, generation context, prompt hash, human involvement, session identifiers, and correlation IDs.
requirement_text.AC.10.2: Verify that origin and generation metadata is checked for completeness and consistency: no missing or ambiguous fields, values normalized to a single representation, and a signature chain that validates back to a trusted root.
requirement_text.AC.11.1: Verify that AI review and assistant bots treat every piece of PR-supplied content (diff, title, description, comments, file contents, commit messages, linked external URLs) as untrusted input, and apply the AISVS C2.1 prompt-injection defenses: instruction-hierarchy enforcement, content sanitization, and indirect-injection detection.
requirement_text.AC.11.2: Verify that AI review and assistant bot system prompts and policy configurations are integrity-checked at load time (signed, hash-pinned), and that nothing in the repository, in branch contents, in PR-sourced environment variables, or in any other user-controllable input can modify them.
requirement_text.AC.11.3: Verify that AI review and assistant bots emit only structured, schema-validated output (JSON with an allow-list of fields and actions). Any free-form output is treated as untrusted and never executed as a command, a query, a shell snippet, or a workflow step.
requirement_text.AC.11.4: Verify that AI review and assistant bots run in network-isolated, least-privilege sandboxes: a dedicated namespace, default-deny egress with an allow-list to approved APIs only, no mounted repository secrets, and ephemeral credentials only.
requirement_text.AC.11.5: Verify that any privileged action a bot can take (approving a PR, merging, labeling, dismissing reviews, posting comments outside its sandbox, invoking external tools) goes through a separate, audited authorization path. That path is adjudicated by a policy engine, not by the LLM.
requirement_text.AC.11.6: Verify that AI review and assistant bots log all prompts (including externally sourced context), tool calls, and outputs to tamper-evident storage. Egress patterns (URLs, IPs, DNS, payload sizes) are continuously monitored for exfiltration indicators, with alerting tuned for webhook, paste-site, and bin-service destinations.
requirement_text.AC.11.7: Verify that AI review bots run in a zero-privilege, read-only shadow mode for untrusted fork PRs. In shadow mode, inline code-generation commentary is restricted and privileged workflow interaction is forbidden, until a repository maintainer has cleared an initial first-time-contributor verification gate.
requirement_text.AC.12.1: Verify that workflows triggered by untrusted contributions (GitHub Actions `pull_request_target`, `workflow_run`, and equivalent fork-aware triggers in other CI systems) never check out, build, test, or otherwise execute untrusted code in a context that has repository write permissions or access to repository, organization, package-registry, cloud, or deployment secrets. Where a privileged follow-up step is needed, the untrusted contribution is first processed in an unprivileged `pull_request` workflow, and only validated passive artifacts are passed forward to a separate privileged workflow.
requirement_text.AC.12.2: Verify that secrets, credentials, and pipeline job tokens are not persisted into workspaces that process AI-touched or fork-originated untrusted code. For example, set `persist-credentials: false` on checkout where the platform supports it, and scrub CI runners of cached credentials before AI tooling runs.
requirement_text.AC.12.3: Verify that secrets are not exposed to workflows running code from forks or first-time contributors. Environment-protection rules (or the platform equivalent, such as protected variables and deployment approvals) require a manual approval before any secret-bearing job runs for those contributions. This control pairs with AC.11.7 and AC.13.2. Bot-level enforcement under AC.11.7 does not substitute for the platform-level enforcement required here.
requirement_text.AC.12.4: Verify that self-hosted or persistent runners used by AI tooling are ephemeral (destroyed after each job), network-segmented, and isolated from production credentials. Persistent or long-lived runners do not process fork PRs or AI-generated untrusted artifacts under any circumstances.
requirement_text.AC.12.5: Verify that changes to workflow definition files (`.github/workflows/*`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Jenkinsfile`, Argo, Tekton, and equivalents) are detected on every PR and route through an elevated review path that includes a security reviewer, regardless of who the contributor is or whether AI was involved. AI agents must not be granted bypass authority over this review path.
requirement_text.AC.12.6: Verify that pipeline audit logs (workflow runs, secret access, runner registration, permission grants, OIDC token issuance) are streamed in real time to centralized security monitoring. Detection rules are tuned for AI-augmented threat patterns: bulk PR creation from new accounts, workflow-file modifications in fork PRs, unexpected secret access from AI-runner pools, and unusual egress (webhooks, paste sites, bin services) from AI workloads.
requirement_text.AC.12.7: Verify that artifacts produced by untrusted PR workflows are treated as untrusted passive data when a privileged follow-up workflow consumes them. The privileged workflow never executes binaries, scripts, packages, caches, or generated workflow fragments that originated in an untrusted contribution.
requirement_text.AC.12.8: Verify that the remediation of a vulnerable workflow includes invalidating or re-validating any PR that was opened before the fix landed. Without this step, a later commit to the same PR can pick up the stale workflow definition and route around the fix.
requirement_text.AC.13.1: Verify that contribution-velocity and contributor-reputation analytics flag anomalies: bulk PR creation from newly created accounts, coordinated fork waves immediately preceding PRs, PR volumes that are inconsistent with human authorship, and reuse of payload patterns across unrelated repositories.
requirement_text.AC.13.2: Verify that PRs from first-time or low-reputation contributors require maintainer approval before any privileged workflow processes them. Privileged workflows here include AI review bots, secret-bearing jobs, and external-integration calls.
requirement_text.AC.13.3: Verify that automated PR pipeline gates detect known indicators of LLM-generated or LLM-assisted malicious payload patterns: registry-confusable or typosquatted dependency names, package references that do not resolve to any published version, and dependencies whose creation, first-publication, or maintainer-change timestamps look anomalous relative to the PR.
requirement_text.AC.13.4: Verify that detection rules are tagged to MITRE ATT&CK (T1195 Supply Chain Compromise and CI/CD-relevant sub-techniques) and to MITRE ATLAS techniques, maintained for the inbound contribution analysis use case, and reviewed against current threat intelligence.
requirement_text.AC.14.1: Verify that an incident-response playbook exists for AI-in-pipeline compromise. At minimum it covers: revoking AI-agent credentials, rotating every secret that touched the compromised workflow run, quarantining the compromised artifacts, notifying downstream consumers, notifying regulators where applicable, and preserving prompts, responses, and audit logs for forensics.
requirement_text.AC.14.2: Verify that any secret that touched a workflow run associated with a suspicious PR, a prompt-injection event, or an AI-agent anomaly is automatically rotated, and that downstream issuers (cloud IAM, package registries, signing-key custodians) are notified of the rotation.
requirement_text.AC.14.3: Verify that AI agent identities (keys, tokens, OIDC trust grants) can be rapidly revoked and quarantined, with a target time-to-revoke that is written down and tested at least once a year.
requirement_text.AC.14.4: Verify that build provenance and AI BOM records are used during incident response to identify every downstream artifact produced under the suspect AI agent or the compromised pipeline run, so that recall, rebuild, or quarantine can be targeted.
requirement_text.AC.2.1: Verify that every AI tool, whether it is an assistant, a reviewer, an agent, or an MCP server, has a threat model. The threat model covers misuse, model inversion, training-data leakage, prompt injection from untrusted input, insecure output handling, excessive agency, and risk inherited from its dependency chain.
requirement_text.AC.2.2: Verify that the evaluation of each tool covers the local components (static and dynamic analysis), the SaaS endpoints (TLS, AuthN/AuthZ, logging, data residency), and the vendor's model supply chain (training-data provenance, fine-tune history, RAG sources). Each of these is reviewed and the review is written down.
requirement_text.AC.2.3: Verify that each tool goes through adversarial robustness testing before onboarding. The testing is repeated after any material change to the model or to the system prompts. Coverage includes automated prompt-injection probes, jailbreak suites, and indirect-injection corpora delivered through realistic PR and issue surfaces.
requirement_text.AC.3.1: Verify that written guidance forbids putting secrets, credentials, PII, or classified data in any prompt sent to an AI tool. The guidance is enforced in pre-commit hooks, IDE integrations, and CI.
requirement_text.AC.3.2: Verify that technical controls automatically strip sensitive material from any context window sent to an AI tool. Client-side redaction, approved context filters, and secret scanners with pre-prompt hooks all qualify.
requirement_text.AC.3.3: Verify that any externally sourced context being fed to an AI tool is treated as untrusted and screened for prompt injection before it reaches the prompt. Sources to cover: PR descriptions and comments, fork-supplied diffs, issue bodies, commit messages, third-party documentation, web search results, and MCP tool outputs.
requirement_text.AC.3.4: Verify that the AI tool enforces an instruction hierarchy, with system and developer messages taking precedence over untrusted repository content. This hierarchy has to hold across multi-turn conversations and tool-augmented workflows.
requirement_text.AC.3.5: Verify that input length controls stop untrusted PR or repository content from crowding system instructions or safety directives out of the effective context window. Oversized inputs are rejected outright. Silent truncation is not acceptable.
requirement_text.AC.4.1: Verify that AI-generated code always goes through code review by a qualified human engineer. The reviewer must not be the same identity that asked for the AI generation in the first place (separation of duties). And the AI agent itself does not count as the human reviewer.
requirement_text.AC.4.2: Verify that automated security testing runs on every pull request containing AI-generated code: SAST, IAST, DAST, secret scanning, IaC scanning, and SCA. Where the scanner supports them, AI-attribution-aware rules are turned on.
requirement_text.AC.4.3: Verify that pull requests containing AI-generated code are blocked from merging when an automated scan surfaces a critical security finding, defined as CVSS >= 9.0 or the equivalent threshold in the organization's vulnerability severity policy. Bypassing the block requires a written exception approved by an authorized human.
requirement_text.AC.4.4: Verify that security-critical files require an elevated review threshold when AI generated or modified them: two-person review, security-team sign-off, or stricter. Security-critical files here include authentication, authorization, and cryptography code; IAM policy; CI/CD workflow definitions; deployment manifests; and sandbox or network policy artifacts.
requirement_text.AC.5.1: Verify that prompt-and-response pairs are logged with stable correlation identifiers, so that an investigator can later replay the whole chain: prompt → response → commit → build → deployment.
requirement_text.AC.6.1: Verify that developers and reviewers can flag insecure or non-compliant suggestions, and that each flag is tracked to closure with links back to the originating prompt and response and forward to any downstream artifacts.
requirement_text.AC.6.2: Verify that aggregated feedback feeds into periodic system-prompt updates or retrieval-augmented generation against vetted secure-coding corpora (OWASP Cheat Sheets, internal coding standards). Where the organization controls model training infrastructure, fine-tuning on the same feedback corpus is also required.
requirement_text.AC.6.3: Verify that scheduled red-team exercises target the AI tooling itself. The exercises include direct and indirect prompt-injection probes delivered through realistic PR, issue, and comment surfaces, jailbreak corpora, and supply-chain payload generation. Findings are remediated under tracked severity SLAs.
requirement_text.AC.7.1: Verify that AI-generated or AI-modified artifacts are clearly labeled and tracked as such. Artifact classes in scope include infrastructure-as-code (Terraform, CloudFormation, Pulumi, Bicep), CI/CD workflow files (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkinsfile, Argo Workflows, Tekton), container and orchestration manifests (Dockerfile, Kubernetes, Helm), and security policy artifacts (IAM, OPA/Rego, NetworkPolicy, admission controllers).
requirement_text.AC.7.2: Verify that AI-generated infrastructure and pipeline configurations require human review and approval before they run in any environment beyond a hermetic sandbox.
requirement_text.AC.7.3: Verify that AI-generated infrastructure and workflow changes pass policy-as-code enforcement (OPA, Conftest, Checkov, tfsec, KICS, kube-linter) at the same level as, or stricter than, human-authored changes. Policy violations block promotion.
requirement_text.AC.7.4: Verify that changes to high-impact pipeline trigger configurations require both dual control and a security-team review, no matter who or what produced the change. The configurations in scope include GitHub Actions `pull_request_target` and `workflow_run`, self-hosted runner labels, workflow `permissions:` blocks, OIDC trust policies, and secret-environment mappings.
requirement_text.AC.8.1: Verify that autonomous agents cannot approve, merge, sign, or deploy artifacts that they themselves generated, and that this constraint is enforced by the source-control system, the CI system, and the artifact registry. Policy alone does not satisfy this control.
requirement_text.AC.8.2: Verify that AI systems run with scoped, non-human identities (service accounts, workload identities, OIDC-issued ephemeral tokens), and that those identities cannot be used to promote their own generated artifacts across environments.
requirement_text.AC.8.3: Verify that autonomous agents cannot bypass branch protection, required reviews, required status checks, signed-commit requirements, or merge queues. Any attempt by an agent to change these settings raises a security alert.
requirement_text.AC.9.1: Verify that AI-generated artifacts carry signed origin and generation metadata (in-toto or SLSA provenance attestations, AI BOM entries) identifying the AI system that produced them, the generation context, the humans involved, and the associated audit records.
requirement_text.C1.1.1: Verify that training data includes only features, attributes, and fields required for the model's stated purpose.
requirement_text.C1.1.2: Verify that an up-to-date inventory is kept of every training-data source, including its origin, responsible party, license, collection method, intended use constraints, and processing history.
requirement_text.C1.1.3: Verify that data integrity is provided when training data is stored and transferred.
requirement_text.C1.1.4: Verify that integrity monitoring is applied to guard against unauthorized modifications or corruption of training data.
requirement_text.C1.2.1: Verify that labeling platforms enforce access controls that restrict who can create, modify, or approve annotations.
requirement_text.C1.2.2: Verify that cryptographic integrity is applied to labeling artifacts.
requirement_text.C1.2.3: Verify that sensitive information in labels is redacted, anonymized, or encrypted before being used in any labeling artifact.
requirement_text.C1.3.1: Verify that training and fine-tuning pipelines implement poisoning detection techniques to identify potential data poisoning or unintentional corruption in training data.
requirement_text.C1.3.2: Verify that automatically generated labels are subject to confidence thresholds and consistency checks to detect misleading or low-confidence labels.
requirement_text.C1.3.3: Verify that models used in security-relevant decisions are evaluated for bias patterns.
requirement_text.C1.3.4: Verify that disallowed content is detected and removed before training.
requirement_text.C10.1.1: Verify that MCP components are obtained only from trusted sources and cryptographically verified.
requirement_text.C10.1.2: Verify that only allow-listed MCP servers are permitted.
requirement_text.C10.1.3: Verify that locally launched MCP servers run in a least-privilege sandbox with restricted file system, network, and system access.
requirement_text.C10.2.1: Verify that MCP servers validate access tokens for each request and do not rely on transport security alone.
requirement_text.C10.2.2: Verify that MCP servers validate the presented access token's issuer, audience, expiration, and scope claims in accordance with OAuth 2.1.
requirement_text.C10.2.3: Verify that MCP servers acting as OAuth 2.1 resource servers do not store or persist access tokens or user credentials.
requirement_text.C10.2.4: Verify that MCP tools/list returns only tools permitted by resource owners' authorized scopes.
requirement_text.C10.2.5: Verify that MCP servers enforce access control on every tool invocation, validating that the user's access token authorizes both the requested tool and the specific argument values supplied.
requirement_text.C10.2.6: Verify that MCP servers ensure all session artifacts are removed when a session terminates.
requirement_text.C10.2.7: Verify that MCP servers do not pass through access tokens received from clients to downstream APIs.
requirement_text.C10.3.1: Verify that authenticated, encrypted streamable HTTP is used for MCP transport for remote services.
requirement_text.C10.3.2: Verify that stdio transport is permitted only in controlled local environments.
requirement_text.C10.3.3: Verify that MCP servers validate both the Origin header and the Host header independently on all HTTP-based transports to prevent DNS rebinding attacks.
requirement_text.C10.3.4: Verify that MCP clients enforce a minimum acceptable protocol version and reject initialize responses that propose a version below that minimum.
requirement_text.C10.4.1: Verify that MCP tools/list and tools/call responses are validated against their declared schemas before being injected into the model context.
requirement_text.C10.4.2: Verify that MCP tools/list and tools/call responses are screened for indirect prompt injection before being injected into the model context.
requirement_text.C10.4.3: Verify that MCP servers reject unrecognized or oversized parameters in function calls.
requirement_text.C10.4.4: Verify that all MCP servers enforce strict schema validation.
requirement_text.C10.4.5: Verify that all MCP transports enforce maximum payload size limits.
requirement_text.C10.4.6: Verify that MCP servers sign tool responses with a unique nonce and timestamp so MCP clients can detect replay attempts.
requirement_text.C10.4.7: Verify that MCP clients present users with explicit consent dialogue and cancellation options upon installation of a local MCP server.
requirement_text.C11.1.1: Verify that the model has undergone alignment and safety training or fine-tuning to prevent the model from generating disallowed content categories.
requirement_text.C11.1.2: Verify that a version-controlled alignment test suite is run on every model update or release.
requirement_text.C11.1.3: Verify that models are evaluated against known adversarial attack techniques relevant to their modality.
requirement_text.C11.1.4: Verify that models are hardened against adversarial inputs.
requirement_text.C11.2.1: Verify that model-inferred sensitive attributes are not directly returned in outputs.
requirement_text.C11.2.2: Verify that inference endpoints enforce per-principal and global rate limits sized to the extraction threat model, and not solely as a generic API throttle.
requirement_text.C11.2.3: Verify that model outputs are calibrated to reduce overconfident predictions.
requirement_text.C11.2.4: Verify that training on sensitive datasets employs differentially-private optimization.
requirement_text.C11.3.1: Verify that query-pattern analysis feeds an extraction-attempt detector.
requirement_text.C11.3.2: Verify that raw model outputs are not directly exposed beyond the application backend, and that externally visible responses are calibrated to the extraction risk level.
requirement_text.C11.4.1: Verify that inputs from external or untrusted sources pass through anomaly detection before model inference.
requirement_text.C11.4.2: Verify that inputs flagged as anomalous trigger gating actions.
requirement_text.C12.1.1: Verify that AI interactions are logged with session context and AI-specific telemetry.
requirement_text.C12.1.2: Verify that safety filtering and policy decisions are logged with sufficient detail to support audit, debugging, and forensic analysis of content moderation systems.
requirement_text.C12.1.3: Verify that log entries for AI inference events follow a structured, interoperable schema that includes at least the model identifier, token usage (input and output), provider name, and operation type.
requirement_text.C12.1.4: Verify that RAG pipeline retrieval events are logged, including the query, documents retrieved, and knowledge source.
requirement_text.C12.2.1: Verify that the system detects and alerts on known jailbreak patterns, prompt injection attempts, and adversarial inputs.
requirement_text.C12.2.2: Verify that behavioral anomaly detection identifies unusual conversation patterns, excessive retry attempts, or probing behaviors.
requirement_text.C12.2.3: Verify that custom rules detect AI-specific threat patterns for coordinated jailbreak attempts, prompt injection, and system prompt extraction attempts.
requirement_text.C12.2.4: Verify that extraction-alert events include offending query metadata to support investigation.
requirement_text.C12.2.5: Verify that token usage is tracked at granular attribution levels including per user, per session, per feature endpoint, and per team or workspace.
requirement_text.C12.3.1: Verify that data drift detection monitors input distribution changes that may impact model performance, using statistically validated methods matched to the input data type (e.g., KS test or PSI for tabular numeric features, embedding-distance metrics for text or image).
requirement_text.C12.3.2: Verify that hallucination detection monitors identify and flag model outputs that contain factually incorrect, inconsistent, or fabricated information.
requirement_text.C12.3.3: Verify that hallucination rates are tracked as continuous time-series metrics to enable trend analysis and detection of sustained model degradation.
requirement_text.C12.4.1: Verify that autonomous action triggers include proactive behavior-pattern analysis, security evaluation, and threat-landscape assessment.
requirement_text.C12.4.2: Verify that audit logs capture security-critical proactive actions, including approver identity, timestamp, action parameters, and decision outcomes.
requirement_text.C12.4.3: Verify that kill-switch activations and override commands are logged.
requirement_text.C12.5.1: Verify that dataset lineage records each dataset and its components, including all transformations, augmentations, and merges.
requirement_text.C12.5.2: Verify that all labeling activities are recorded in logs.
requirement_text.C12.5.3: Verify that all model changes generate immutable audit records.
requirement_text.C12.5.4: Verify that every ingested document is tagged at write time with source, writer identity, and timestamp.
requirement_text.C2.1.1: Verify that input normalization is applied before tokenization or embedding.
requirement_text.C2.1.2: Verify that encoding and representation smuggling in inputs is detected and mitigated. Approved mitigations include canonicalization, strict schema validation, policy-based rejection, or explicit marking.
requirement_text.C2.1.3: Verify that all inputs that could steer model behavior are treated as untrusted and screened by a prompt injection detection ruleset or classifier, with flagged inputs blocked.
requirement_text.C2.1.4: Verify that input length controls prevent content from exceeding the context window. The controls must reject inputs that exceed token limits rather than truncating them.
requirement_text.C2.1.5: Verify that the system implements a character set restriction for all inputs. The restriction must use an allow-list approach that permits only characters that are explicitly required.
requirement_text.C2.1.6: Verify that the system enforces an instruction hierarchy in which system and developer messages override user instructions and other untrusted inputs, even after user instructions have been processed.
requirement_text.C2.1.7: Verify that reserved special tokens are encoded as literal characters and cannot be injected into the model context.
requirement_text.C2.2.1: Verify that every prompt is scored by a content classifier for violence, self-harm, hate, and sexual content against configurable thresholds. Prompts that exceed those thresholds are rejected or sanitized before reaching the model context.
requirement_text.C2.2.2: Verify that prompt content classification is evaluated for unsupported languages.
requirement_text.C2.2.3: Verify that non-text inputs (image/video/audio) are checked for adversarial perturbations, steganographic payloads, hidden or embedded content, or known attack patterns.
requirement_text.C3.1.1: Verify that a model registry maintains an inventory of all deployed model artifacts and their origin.
requirement_text.C3.1.2: Verify that all model artifacts (weights, configurations, tokenizers, base models, fine-tunes, adapters, and safety/policy models) are cryptographically signed by authorized entities.
requirement_text.C3.1.3: Verify that model cryptographic signatures are verified at deployment admission and on load.
requirement_text.C3.2.1: Verify that models undergo automated input validation testing, safety evaluation testing, and output sanitization testing before deployment.
requirement_text.C3.2.2: Verify that models subjected to post-training quantization are re-evaluated against the same safety and alignment test suite on the compressed artifact before deployment.
requirement_text.C3.3.1: Verify that production deployments implement rollout mechanisms with automated rollback triggers.
requirement_text.C3.3.2: Verify that rollback capabilities restore the complete model state.
requirement_text.C3.3.3: Verify that model versions running in parallel use isolated runtime state so that AI-specific shared resources are not shared across deployments.
requirement_text.C3.4.1: Verify that AI-specific runtime components are not shared across environment boundaries (e.g., development, staging, production).
requirement_text.C3.4.2: Verify that model training and fine-tuning environments are isolated from production environments.
requirement_text.C3.5.1: Verify that models used in RLHF fine-tuning are versioned and integrity-verified before use in a training run.
requirement_text.C4.1.1: Verify that AI models execute in isolated sandboxes.
requirement_text.C4.1.2: Verify that model artifact loading enforces an explicit allow-list of serialization formats that do not permit arbitrary code execution during deserialization.
requirement_text.C4.2.1: Verify that AI accelerator (GPU) firmware is version-pinned, signed, and attested at boot.
requirement_text.C4.3.1: Verify that edge AI devices authenticate to central infrastructure using strong authentication mechanisms.
requirement_text.C4.3.2: Verify that models deployed to edge or mobile devices are cryptographically signed during packaging, and that the on-device runtime validates these signatures or checksums before loading or inference.
requirement_text.C5.2.1: Verify that every AI resource (datasets, endpoints, vector collections, embedding indices, compute instances) enforces access controls with explicit allow-lists and default-deny policies.
requirement_text.C5.2.2: Verify that retrieval pipelines (e.g., RAG queries, embedding lookups) enforce the end-user's authorization context at each retrieval and assembly stage, rather than relying solely on the service account's permissions.
requirement_text.C5.2.3: Verify that sensitive data is retrieved via retrieval pipelines (e.g., RAG queries, embedding lookups) to prevent permanent storage in models.
requirement_text.C5.2.4: Verify that post-inference filtering mechanisms prevent responses from including data that the requester is not authorized to receive.
requirement_text.C5.2.5: Verify that the policy decision point for agent authorization is isolated from the agent's execution environment.
requirement_text.C5.3.1: Verify that shared model serving infrastructure prevents one tenant's fine-tuning, inference, or embedding operations from influencing or observing another tenant's operations.
requirement_text.C6.1.1: Verify that models are scanned for malicious code before import.
requirement_text.C6.1.2: Verify that model weights, datasets, and fine-tuning adapters are downloaded only from approved sources.
requirement_text.C6.1.3: Verify that every third-party model artifact can be integrity-verified.
requirement_text.C6.1.4: Verify that models pass a behavioral acceptance test suite before being promoted to any non-development environment.
requirement_text.C6.2.1: Verify that every model artifact publishes a version-controlled, machine-readable AI BOM listing datasets, weights, licenses, and data-origin statements.
requirement_text.C6.2.2: Verify that AI BOMs are cryptographically signed before deployment.
requirement_text.C6.2.3: Verify that AI BOM completeness checks fail the build if any component metadata is missing.
requirement_text.C7.1.1: Verify that the application validates all model outputs against a defined schema and rejects any output that does not match.
requirement_text.C7.1.2: Verify that model-generated output is bounded by length limits and termination controls.
requirement_text.C7.2.1: Verify that the system assesses the reliability of generated answers using a confidence estimation method.
requirement_text.C7.2.2: Verify that the application automatically blocks answers or switches to a fallback message if the confidence score drops below a defined threshold.
requirement_text.C7.3.1: Verify that automated classifiers scan every response and block content that matches defined harmful content categories.
requirement_text.C7.3.2: Verify that output filters detect and block responses that disclose system prompt content or backend data.
requirement_text.C7.3.3: Verify that model-generated output is prevented from triggering outbound requests.
requirement_text.C7.4.1: Verify that responses generated using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) include attribution to the source documents.
requirement_text.C7.4.2: Verify that RAG attributions are derived from retrieval metadata and are not generated by the model, so provenance cannot be fabricated.
requirement_text.C7.4.3: Verify that claims in a RAG response can be traced to the retrieved chunk.
requirement_text.C8.1.1: Verify that vector identifiers and namespaces enforce uniqueness per tenant and prevent cross-tenant collisions.
requirement_text.C8.1.2: Verify that document metadata tags are immutable after the initial write.
requirement_text.C8.1.3: Verify that retrieval operations enforce scope constraints.
requirement_text.C8.2.1: Verify that sensitive fields are detected before embedding and are masked, tokenized, or dropped.
requirement_text.C8.2.2: Verify that vectors that fall outside normal clustering patterns are flagged and quarantined before entering production indices.
requirement_text.C8.2.3: Verify that agent outputs and tool outputs are not automatically written to trusted agent memory without explicit source validation.
requirement_text.C8.3.1: Verify that expired vectors are excluded from retrieval results.
requirement_text.C8.3.2: Verify that memory can be reset.
requirement_text.C9.1.1: Verify that per-tool quotas and timeouts (e.g., CPU, memory, disk, egress, and execution time) are enforced.
requirement_text.C9.1.2: Verify that per-execution budgets (e.g., max recursion depth, token use, and monetary spend) are configured and enforced by the runtime.
requirement_text.C9.1.3: Verify that a swarm-level kill-switch exists that can halt all active agent instances.
requirement_text.C9.2.1: Verify that the agent runtime blocks execution of privileged, high-impact, or irreversible actions until explicit human approval is received and verified.
requirement_text.C9.2.2: Verify that approval requests display canonicalized and complete action parameters, such as diffs, commands, recipients, amounts, resources, and scopes, without truncation or unsafe transformation.
requirement_text.C9.2.3: Verify that each high-impact action has a trusted reversibility classification, such as read-only, reversible, externally reversible, or irreversible.
requirement_text.C9.2.4: Verify that the agent runtime enforces reversibility classifications by blocking, requiring approval, or restricting actions based on their impact and ability to be reversed.
requirement_text.C9.2.5: Verify that any self-modification capability (e.g., prompt rewriting, tool-list changes, parameter updates) is restricted by enforceable boundaries.
requirement_text.C9.2.6: Verify that agentic systems include an AI-augmented review of planned high-risk actions before execution that adds to, and does not replace, the deterministic policy gate.
requirement_text.C9.2.7: Verify that the AI-augmented review mechanism is protected against manipulation by adversarial inputs, and cannot be overridden or bypassed through prompt injection.
requirement_text.C9.3.1: Verify that each tool/plugin executes in a least-privilege sandbox or is otherwise isolated from model operations.
requirement_text.C9.3.2: Verify that tool outputs are validated against schemas.
requirement_text.C9.3.3: Verify that tool manifests declare required privileges, resource limits, and output validation requirements.
requirement_text.C9.3.4: Verify that the runtime enforces the privileges, resource limits, and output-validation requirements declared in tool manifests.
requirement_text.C9.3.5: Verify that components processing untrusted data are isolated from tool-calling capabilities, ensuring that compromised data processing cannot trigger unauthorized tool invocations.
requirement_text.C9.3.6: Verify that there is architectural separation between processing of untrusted tool outputs and agent operations.
requirement_text.C9.3.7: Verify that external resources named in model output are verified against an approved allow-list or registry before the agent installs or invokes them.
requirement_text.C9.4.1: Verify that each agent instance has a unique cryptographic identity and authenticates as a first-class principal to downstream systems.
requirement_text.C9.4.2: Verify that agent-initiated actions are cryptographically bound to each step of the execution chain for non-repudiation.
requirement_text.C9.5.1: Verify that agent actions are authorized against fine-grained policies enforced by the runtime that restrict which tools an agent may invoke, and which parameter values it may supply.
requirement_text.C9.5.2: Verify that when an agent acts on a user's behalf, the runtime propagates an integrity-protected, scope-limited token that carries the user's authorization context and is enforced at every downstream call.
requirement_text.C9.5.3: Verify that all access control decisions are enforced by application logic or a policy engine, never by the AI model itself.
requirement_text.C9.5.4: Verify that secrets and credentials required by an agent at runtime are not exposed within the model's observable context, including the context window, system prompts, or tool call parameters.
requirement_text.C9.5.5: Verify that inter-agent task delegation is restricted by an explicit authorization policy.
requirement_text.C9.6.1: Verify that a manual kill-switch mechanism exists to immediately halt AI model inference and outputs.
requirement_text.C9.6.2: Verify that when a human-approval gate is not satisfied within the defined approval time, the system blocks the pending action.
requirement_text.SBD-AC-01: All communications use TLS/mTLS; service identity is verified (e.g., mesh-issued certs).
requirement_text.SBD-AC-02: Central IdP (OIDC/OAuth2) is used; MFA enforced on privileged/admin paths; tokens are short-lived.
requirement_text.SBD-AC-03: RBAC/ABAC governs APIs and publish/consume on messaging; least privilege is applied.
requirement_text.SBD-AC-04: Authorization is centralized at gateway/mesh via policy-as-code; shared integration services are governed.
requirement_text.SBD-AC-05: Secrets are stored in a secret manager; keys/certs rotate automatically; no secrets in code/logs.
requirement_text.SBD-AC-06: Applicable regulatory controls (e.g., privacy/financial) are identified with evidence of design alignment.
requirement_text.SBD-AC-07: Least privilege extends to CI/CD, VCS apps, chat-ops, and third-party tooling; periodic reviews are scheduled.
requirement_text.SBD-AS-01: Trust zones (logical network "Spaces") are enforced; cross-zone traffic flows only via governed integration layers (gateway/bus).
requirement_text.SBD-AS-02: Service addressing & discovery are unified and consistent across environments; intra-zone shortcuts are not used externally.
requirement_text.SBD-AS-03: Service boundaries are clear; no circular dependencies; services are right-sized; each service owns its data.
